title: Total Alkalinity — Titration Method
frequency: Per shift on raw and treated water, or per treatment programme schedule
holdingTime: Analyse within 24 h; store at 4 °C, fill bottle completely with no headspace
equipment: Burette (25 or 50 mL) or Hach digital titrator
100 mL volumetric pipette or graduated cylinder
Magnetic stirrer and stir bar (optional but recommended)
pH meter with calibrated electrode (preferred over indicators)
reagents: 0.02 N (0.02 mol/L) sulfuric acid titrant — standardised
interferences: Free residual chlorine above ~3 mg/L can bleach indicators — add 1 drop 0.1 N sodium thiosulfate to destroy it.
Highly coloured or turbid samples obscure the indicator endpoint — use the pH meter method instead.
Dissolved CO2 will change during handling: do not filter, dilute, or agitate the sample more than necessary, and keep the bottle capped until analysis.
steps: Verify the titrant is in date and standardised. Record the exact normality on the bench sheet — it is a direct multiplier in the result.
If using a pH meter, calibrate it with pH 7.00 and pH 4.00 buffers and verify the slope is within acceptance (typically 95-105 %).
Rinse the burette twice with a small volume of titrant, fill, and set the meniscus to the zero mark with no air bubbles in the tip.
Measure exactly 100 mL of well-mixed sample into a clean 250 mL flask. For high-alkalinity samples (> 500 mg/L), use 50 mL and note the volume used.

PHENOLPHTHALEIN (P) ALKALINITY — only if pH > 8.3: add 2-3 drops of phenolphthalein indicator. A pink colour confirms P alkalinity is present. Titrate slowly with standard acid, swirling constantly, until the pink colour just disappears (pH 8.3). Record this volume as P.
TOTAL (M) ALKALINITY: add 2-3 drops of bromcresol green-methyl red indicator to the same flask (or continue monitoring with the pH meter).

Continue titrating dropwise, swirling after each drop, until the colour changes from blue-green to a light pink/salmon — or until the pH meter reads exactly 4.5. Approach the endpoint slowly; the last 1 mL should be added drop by drop.
Record the TOTAL titrant volume used from zero (this includes any volume used to reach the P endpoint).
Enter the sample volume, total titrant volume, and titrant normality into the Total Alkalinity calculator.
Log the result, the sample point, the time, and the titrant lot/normality in the Logbook.
Rinse all glassware with distilled water immediately after use; residual acid will bias the next sample low.
qualityControl: Run a reagent blank (100 mL distilled water) — should require essentially zero titrant.
Run a duplicate on every 10th sample; duplicates should agree within about 5 %.
Verify the acid titrant against a known standard (e.g. sodium carbonate) at the interval set by your QA programme.
Investigate any result that differs from the previous shift by more than the site's control limit before reporting it.
troubleshooting: Endpoint colour returns after a few seconds: the endpoint was passed too quickly — CO2 is re-equilibrating. Repeat with slower titration near the endpoint.
Result drifting high over successive runs: check for contaminated glassware or a diluted/degraded titrant.
No colour change at all: verify the indicator has not expired and that the correct indicator was used for the endpoint being targeted.
safetyNotes: Sulfuric acid causes severe burns — wear safety glasses, gloves, and a lab coat.
Always add acid to water, never the reverse, when preparing dilutions.
Know the location of the nearest eyewash station before starting.

title: Total, Calcium, and Magnesium Hardness — EDTA Titration
frequency: Daily on softener outlet and boiler makeup; per shift where hardness breakthrough is a risk
equipment: 250 mL Erlenmeyer flasks (two — one per titration)
Magnetic stirrer (recommended for seeing the endpoint clearly)
reagents: EDTA titrant, 0.01 mol/L (standardised — note the titre in mg CaCO3 per mL)
Buffer solution, pH 10 (ammonia/ammonium chloride) — for total hardness
Eriochrome Black T indicator (ManVer or powder) — for total hardness
1 N sodium hydroxide — for calcium hardness
interferences: Iron, manganese, copper, and aluminium can cause a fading or indistinct endpoint — add an inhibitor (e.g. Hach Inhibitor Solution) if metals are present.
Free chlorine can bleach the indicator — neutralise with a drop of thiosulfate.
Titrating too slowly at high pH lets calcium carbonate precipitate; complete each titration within 5 minutes of adding buffer.
steps: TOTAL HARDNESS — measure exactly 100 mL of sample into a flask (use 50 mL and note it if hardness is expected above 300 mg/L).
Add 1-2 mL of pH 10 buffer solution and swirl. Work in a ventilated area; the buffer has a strong ammonia odour.
Add the Eriochrome Black T indicator. The solution turns wine-red if hardness is present.

Titrate with EDTA, swirling continuously, until the colour changes from wine-red through purple to a clear blue with no red tint remaining. Add the last few drops slowly, allowing 3-5 seconds between drops.
Record the EDTA volume used for total hardness.
CALCIUM HARDNESS — measure a fresh 100 mL sample into a second clean flask.
Add 1-2 mL of 1 N sodium hydroxide to raise the pH to 12-13. At this pH magnesium precipitates as hydroxide and is excluded from the titration.
Add murexide (calcium) indicator; the solution turns pink.
Titrate with EDTA until the colour changes from pink to purple. Complete this titration promptly — the endpoint fades on standing.
Record the EDTA volume used for calcium hardness.
Enter both titrant volumes, the sample volume, and the EDTA titre into the Hardness calculator. Magnesium hardness is returned by difference (total − calcium).
Log all three results plus the sample point and time in the Logbook. A rising trend on a softener outlet is an early warning of resin exhaustion.
qualityControl: Run a known hardness standard with each batch; recovery should be within about ±5 % of the assigned value.
Run a duplicate on every 10th sample.
Run a distilled water blank — it should require essentially no titrant.
For softened water, any detectable hardness above the site limit should be repeated immediately on a fresh sample before raising an alarm.
troubleshooting: Endpoint is grey/muddy rather than clear blue: metal interference — add inhibitor and repeat.
Colour reverts to red shortly after the endpoint: hardness is still being released; titrate more slowly and confirm the buffer volume.
Very sharp endpoint at almost zero titrant on softened water: confirm with a standard that the indicator and titrant are both still good.
safetyNotes: Sodium hydroxide is caustic and causes severe burns — gloves and eye protection required.
pH 10 buffer releases ammonia vapour — use in a fume hood or well-ventilated area.
Avoid skin contact with indicator powders.

title: Chlorine, Free & Total — Hach DPD (DR6000)
methodRef: Hach Method 8021 (free) / 8167 (total) — DPD colorimetric; equivalent to SM 4500-Cl G
hachMethod: Method 8021 (free chlorine) / Method 8167 (total chlorine) — DPD powder pillows
range: 0.02 – 2.00 mg/L Cl2 (10 mL cell); dilute for higher concentrations
reactionTime: Free: read within 1 minute. Total: 3 minute reaction, read within 3 minutes after
wavelength: 530 nm (set automatically by the stored program)
frequency: Per shift minimum on treated water; more often during disinfection upsets
holdingTime: ANALYSE IMMEDIATELY — chlorine is unstable. Do not store or transport samples.
equipment: Matched 10 mL sample cells (round, 1 inch) — use the same pair every time
reagents: DPD Free Chlorine Powder Pillows, 10 mL
DPD Total Chlorine Powder Pillows, 10 mL
Deionised water for the blank (if a reagent blank is required)
interferences: Monochloramine gives a slowly developing colour in the free chlorine test — read within 1 minute to minimise this.
Oxidised manganese and chromium give a positive interference.
Sample temperature and pH outside the method's range shift results; samples should be near ambient temperature.
Excess chlorine (above range) can bleach the pink colour and give a falsely LOW or even near-zero reading — always dilute and re-test if a high-chlorine sample reads unexpectedly low.
steps: Collect the sample in a clean bottle, filling gently and completely to avoid agitating off chlorine. Do not use a sample that has been standing.

Power on the DR6000 and let it complete its self-check. Select the stored program for the test being run (free or total chlorine). Confirm the program number on the instrument — program numbers vary by firmware version; the Hach method number is the stable reference.
PREPARE THE BLANK: fill a clean sample cell to the 10 mL mark with the untreated sample.
Wipe the outside of the cell with a lint-free wipe. Fingerprints, droplets, and scratches all bias the reading.
Insert the blank into the cell holder with the orientation/fill mark aligned consistently, close the lid, and press ZERO. The display should read 0.00 mg/L.
PREPARE THE SAMPLE: fill the second cell to the 10 mL mark with sample.
Add the contents of one DPD powder pillow (free or total, as appropriate). Cap the cell.

Swirl or invert gently for about 20 seconds to dissolve. Do not shake vigorously — this drives off chlorine and traps bubbles. A pink colour indicates chlorine is present. Some undissolved powder is normal and does not affect the result.
FREE CHLORINE: start the instrument timer and read immediately — the reading must be taken within 1 minute of adding reagent.
TOTAL CHLORINE: start the 3-minute instrument timer and read when it expires; take the reading within 3 minutes after the timer ends.
Wipe the prepared cell, insert it in the same orientation as the blank, close the lid, and press READ. Record the result in mg/L as Cl2.
If the reading is over range, dilute a fresh sample with a known ratio of deionised water, re-run the test, and use the Chlorine Residual calculator to apply the dilution factor.
COMBINED CHLORINE (chloramines), if needed: run both tests on the same sample and subtract — combined = total − free.
Empty, rinse, and dry both cells immediately. DPD stains cells over time; clean with a mild acid rinse periodically.
Log the result, sample point, and time in the Logbook, and flag any result outside the target residual band.
qualityControl: Run a blank check periodically using deionised water plus reagent — should read near 0.00 mg/L.
Verify performance against a Hach chlorine standard (e.g. a sealed Gelex or a prepared standard) on the schedule set by your QA programme.
Run duplicates on one sample per shift; agreement should be well within the method's stated precision.
Keep the matched cell pair together and marked — mixing cells between the blank and sample introduces optical error.
troubleshooting: Result reads 0.00 on a sample known to be chlorinated: suspect over-range bleaching. Dilute and re-test.
Erratic or drifting readings: check for bubbles, scratched or dirty cells, or an unstable lamp — let the instrument warm up fully.
Persistent high blank: cells are contaminated with DPD residue; clean thoroughly or replace.
Colour develops slowly and keeps rising on the free test: chloramines are present — the total chlorine test will show the difference.
safetyNotes: DPD reagent is a skin and eye irritant — avoid contact and wash hands after handling.
Dispose of spent samples and reagent per site chemical waste procedure.
The definitive reference is the Hach method sheet supplied with your reagent lot; this SOP is a bench summary.

title: Turbidity — Nephelometric Method
frequency: Continuous on-line where fitted, plus bench verification per shift on raw, settled, and filtered water
holdingTime: Analyse immediately; if unavoidable, store in the dark up to 24 h and bring to room temperature before reading
equipment: Bench or portable nephelometric turbidimeter (e.g. Hach TL2300 / 2100Q)
interferences: Air bubbles read as turbidity — the single most common source of false high results.
Scratched, dirty, or fingerprinted cells scatter light and bias results high.
True colour in the sample absorbs light and can bias results LOW.
Settling of large particles during the reading gives a falling, unstable value.
steps: Verify the instrument calibration is current. Perform a full calibration with StablCal standards at the frequency required by your QA programme, and a verification check daily.
Collect the sample in a clean container, filling gently to minimise entrained air.
Invert the sample slowly several times to homogenise — do not shake, which introduces bubbles.
Let the sample stand briefly (typically 1-5 minutes) so bubbles rise out, but not long enough for solids to settle.
Rinse the sample cell twice with the sample, then fill to the mark and cap.
Wipe the cell with a lint-free cloth. Apply a thin film of silicone oil and wipe with the oiling cloth to mask minor scratches — this is required for low-level readings.
Insert the cell in the instrument with the orientation mark aligned the same way every time and close the light shield.
Read and record the value in NTU. If the reading drifts, note whether it is rising (bubbles) or falling (settling) and repeat as needed.
For very low turbidity (filtered water), take three readings and average, or use the instrument's signal-averaging mode.
Log the result against the sample point and compare to the site's filter performance target — a rising filtered-water turbidity trend is an early indicator of filter breakthrough.
Note: the DR6000 can read attenuated-radiation turbidity (Hach Method 8237, in FAU) for process checks, but a dedicated nephelometer is required for regulatory NTU reporting.
qualityControl: Run a daily calibration verification with a mid-range StablCal standard; record pass/fail.
Run a turbidity-free water blank to confirm the low end reads near zero.
Replace scratched cells immediately — they cannot be corrected with oil.
Track calibration dates and standard expiry in the Logbook.
troubleshooting: Reading climbs steadily: air bubbles — degas the sample and re-read.
Reading falls steadily: solids settling — re-invert and read promptly.
Filtered water reads higher than expected: check the cell for scratches and confirm with a second clean cell.
All readings biased high after a standard change: re-verify the calibration and check standard expiry.
safetyNotes: Formazin stock standards are a suspected carcinogen — use pre-made StablCal standards where possible and avoid preparing formazin from raw materials.

title: pH — Electrometric Method
frequency: Per shift on all key sample points; calibrate the meter daily before first use
holdingTime: ANALYSE IMMEDIATELY — pH changes on standing as CO2 equilibrates
equipment: Combination pH electrode in good condition
Electrode storage solution (never plain distilled water)
interferences: Temperature affects both the electrode response and the true pH of the sample — always use ATC and record the temperature.
A dried-out or coated electrode gives a sluggish, drifting reading.
Low-ionic-strength water (condensate, demineralised water) is difficult to measure accurately — readings drift and require a specialised low-conductivity electrode.
Sodium error at high pH (> 12) biases readings low with older glass electrodes.
steps: Inspect the electrode: the bulb should be clean and free of cracks, the fill solution at the correct level, and the junction unblocked.
Rinse the electrode with distilled water and blot gently with a lint-free tissue — never wipe hard, which creates a static charge.
CALIBRATE with at least two buffers that bracket the expected sample pH (typically 7.00 first, then 4.00 or 10.00).
Allow the reading to stabilise fully in each buffer before accepting the calibration point.
Check the slope reported by the meter. A slope of 95-105 % is normally acceptable; below that, clean or replace the electrode.
Rinse the electrode between every buffer and every sample.
MEASURE: immerse the electrode in the sample so the bulb and junction are fully covered. Stir gently and consistently, or use a stirrer at a constant speed.
Allow the reading to stabilise (the meter's stability indicator should confirm), then record pH to two decimal places along with the sample temperature.
Rinse the electrode and return it to storage solution. Never store the electrode dry or in distilled water — both damage the junction.
Log the pH, temperature, sample point, and the calibration slope from that day in the Logbook.
qualityControl: Verify calibration against a third buffer (a check standard) after calibrating — it should read within ±0.05 pH of nominal.
Record the electrode slope daily; a downward trend predicts electrode failure before it causes bad data.
Re-calibrate immediately if the check standard fails, the electrode is replaced, or a large temperature change occurs.
Replace buffers on schedule — opened buffer bottles absorb CO2 and drift, especially pH 10.
troubleshooting: Slow, drifting reading: clean the electrode, check the fill level, and confirm the junction is not blocked.
Slope out of range: soak the electrode in cleaning solution, then in storage solution, and re-calibrate. If it still fails, replace it.
Noisy reading in demineralised water or condensate: use a low-ionic-strength electrode and a grounded, stirred cell.
Reading offset in all buffers: check the meter's calibration has actually been saved and that ATC is connected.
safetyNotes: Buffers are generally low hazard but should not be returned to the stock bottle after use — always pour a fresh aliquot into a beaker.

title: Total Dissolved Solids — Conductivity & Gravimetric
frequency: Conductivity per shift; gravimetric TDS monthly (or per schedule) to verify the conversion factor
holdingTime: 7 days at 4 °C for gravimetric; conductivity best measured fresh at a known temperature
equipment: Glass fibre filter and filtration apparatus
interferences: The conductivity-to-TDS factor is water-specific — a factor derived for one source is not valid for another.
Temperature strongly affects conductivity (roughly 2 % per °C); always use temperature compensation.
Highly alkaline or acidic samples deviate from the typical factor.
In the gravimetric method, hygroscopic residues regain moisture rapidly — weigh immediately after desiccation.
steps: ROUTINE (CONDUCTIVITY) METHOD — calibrate the conductivity meter against a standard solution and verify it reads within tolerance.
Rinse the probe with deionised water, then with a small volume of sample.
Immerse the probe fully, ensuring no bubbles are trapped in the cell, and allow the reading to stabilise.
Record the conductivity in µS/cm and the sample temperature.
Enter the conductivity and your site-specific factor into the TDS from Conductivity calculator. The 0.65 default is a starting point only — it must be verified gravimetrically for your water.
REFERENCE (GRAVIMETRIC) METHOD — heat a clean evaporating dish at 180 °C for 1 h, cool in a desiccator, and weigh to constant mass. Record the tare.
Filter a measured volume of well-mixed sample through a glass fibre filter to remove suspended solids.
Transfer a measured volume of the filtrate to the tared dish and evaporate to dryness on a water bath or in the oven.
Dry the dish and residue at 180 °C for at least 1 h.
Cool in a desiccator to room temperature and weigh promptly. Repeat the drying/cooling/weighing cycle until successive masses agree within 0.5 mg (constant mass).
Calculate TDS (mg/L) = (final mass − tare mass in mg) × 1000 / sample volume in mL.
DERIVE THE FACTOR: divide the gravimetric TDS (mg/L) by the conductivity (µS/cm) measured on the same sample. Update the factor stored in the calculator and record the change in the Logbook.
qualityControl: Verify conductivity calibration daily against a standard; record the reading and any adjustment.
Run gravimetric duplicates; agreement should be within about 5 %.
Re-derive the conductivity-to-TDS factor whenever the source water changes character (seasonal shifts, new source, process change).
Verify the oven temperature with an independent thermometer periodically.
troubleshooting: Conductivity reads low and slow: probe fouled or bubbles trapped in the cell — clean and re-immerse.
Gravimetric result will not reach constant mass: the residue is hygroscopic; extend the drying time and minimise time outside the desiccator.
Large mismatch between conductivity estimate and gravimetric result: the conversion factor is out of date for this water.
safetyNotes: Use tongs and heat-resistant gloves for hot dishes; a 180 °C dish looks identical to a cold one.
Never place a hot dish directly on the balance — always cool in a desiccator first.

title: Aluminium, Residual — Hach Aluminon (DR6000)
sampleVolume: Per the Hach procedure for this method (verify on the instrument program)
frequency: Daily on filtered/treated water where alum or PAC coagulant is dosed
holdingTime: Analyse promptly; if storage is needed, acidify to pH < 2 with nitric acid (total aluminium only)
reagents: Aluminon reagent powder pillows / AluVer reagent set
interferences: Iron interferes strongly — the ascorbic acid step is included specifically to suppress it and must not be skipped.
Fluoride and polyphosphates suppress colour development and bias results LOW.
The colour is temperature-sensitive; the blank and sample must be at the same temperature.
steps: Collect a representative sample of filtered/treated water in a clean container.
Select the stored program for aluminium (Hach Method 8012) on the DR6000 and confirm the program matches the reagent set in use.
Prepare the sample and blank exactly as directed by the Hach method sheet for your reagent set, including the ascorbic acid interference-removal step.
Use the instrument's built-in timer for each reaction period — do not estimate the timing by eye.
Wipe both cells with a lint-free wipe before every insertion; at this concentration range, fingerprints matter.
Zero the instrument on the blank, then read the prepared sample and record the result in mg/L Al.
Compare the result to your treated-water target. Rising residual aluminium usually signals coagulant overdose or pH drift outside the coagulation optimum — re-check the jar test and coagulation pH.
Log the result, the coagulant dose in use, and the coagulation pH together in the Logbook so the relationship is visible over time.
qualityControl: Run a reagent blank with each batch of samples.
Verify against a prepared aluminium standard on the QA schedule; recovery should fall within the method's stated limits.
Run a duplicate on every 10th sample.
Confirm reagent lot and expiry are recorded.
troubleshooting: Unexpectedly low result on a known-high sample: check for fluoride/polyphosphate interference and confirm the reaction timing.
High blank: cells are contaminated — clean thoroughly with acid rinse.
Poor reproducibility: verify both cells are at the same temperature and the timer was used consistently.
safetyNotes: Aluminon reagent is an irritant — avoid skin and eye contact.
The definitive reference is the Hach method sheet for your reagent lot; this SOP is a bench summary.

title: Jar Test — Coagulant Dose Optimisation
methodRef: Standard bench jar test practice (ASTM D2035 basis)
frequency: Weekly, and whenever raw water quality shifts (rain event, turbidity spike, temperature change, source change)
equipment: Jar test apparatus (gang stirrer, typically 6 paddles)
1 or 2 L square/round jars, matched set
reagents: Coagulant stock solution of accurately known strength (prepare fresh; note the concentration)
pH adjustment chemicals as used on the plant (lime, caustic, acid)
interferences: Stale stock solutions give misleading doses — prepare coagulant stock fresh, especially dilute solutions.
Raw water that has stood or warmed does not represent plant conditions; test as soon after collection as possible.
Uneven paddle speeds across jars invalidate the comparison — verify all paddles are turning at the same rate.
steps: Collect a large, well-mixed raw water sample from the plant intake at the point representative of current conditions.
Record the raw water turbidity, pH, temperature, and alkalinity before starting — these drive interpretation of the result.
Fill each jar with an identical measured volume of raw water (typically 1 or 2 L).
Plan the dose series: include one blank/control (no coagulant) and 5 doses bracketing the current plant dose — for example, if the plant runs 30 mg/L, test 15, 22, 30, 38, 45 mg/L.
Calculate the volume of stock solution needed for each jar to achieve the target mg/L and draw it up in advance so all jars can be dosed simultaneously.
Start the stirrers at RAPID MIX (typically ~100-150 rpm) and add all doses at the same instant. Rapid mix for 1 minute.

Reduce to SLOW MIX (typically ~20-40 rpm) for 15-20 minutes to build floc. Observe and record floc appearance during this phase: time to first visible floc, floc size, and whether the floc is compact or fluffy.
If a polymer aid is being evaluated, add it partway through the slow mix as the plant would dose it, and note the addition point.

Stop the stirrers, lift the paddles clear, and let the jars settle undisturbed for 30 minutes. Record the settling behaviour — fast, clean settling versus slow, cloudy settling is as informative as the final number.
Withdraw supernatant from a consistent depth in each jar (typically 2-3 cm below the surface) using a pipette or siphon, taking care not to disturb the settled sludge.
Measure and record turbidity for each jar, and pH for at least the best two jars.
Enter the dose/turbidity pairs into the Jar Test calculator to identify the lowest-turbidity dose.

Interpret before acting: the optimum operating dose is usually the LOWEST dose that reaches acceptable turbidity, not necessarily the absolute minimum turbidity — the last few mg/L often buys very little and costs chemical.
Check the coagulation pH of the winning jar. If it falls outside the coagulant's optimum range, the dose result may be masking a pH problem; re-run with pH adjustment.
Use the Coagulant Dose Scale-Up calculator to convert the chosen mg/L dose to kg/day at current plant flow, then the Feed Pump Rate calculator for the pump setting.
Log the full jar test — raw water conditions, dose series, turbidity results, chosen dose, and any plant change made — in the Logbook.
qualityControl: Always include a no-coagulant control jar to confirm how much settling occurs without treatment.
Verify all paddles rotate at the same speed before starting.
Record the stock solution concentration and preparation date on every jar test record.
Repeat the test if the turbidity results do not form a sensible curve (a proper series should show a clear minimum, not random scatter).
troubleshooting: No clear minimum in the curve: the dose range may be entirely too low or too high — widen the series and repeat.
All jars settle poorly including high doses: check coagulation pH and alkalinity; insufficient alkalinity prevents floc formation.
Pinpoint floc that will not grow: consider a flocculant aid, or a longer/gentler slow-mix phase.
Best jar in the test is still above target turbidity: the issue may be filtration rather than coagulation.
safetyNotes: Follow the safety data sheet for each coagulant and polymer — many are acidic and corrosive.
Polymer solutions make floors extremely slippery; clean spills immediately.
Wear eye protection when preparing and dispensing stock solutions.

title: Chemical Feed Pump Calibration (Drawdown)
frequency: Monthly per pump, and after any stroke/speed adjustment, pump repair, or chemical change
equipment: Graduated calibration column (drawdown cylinder) plumbed to the pump suction
PPE appropriate to the chemical being pumped
interferences: Air in the suction line gives a falsely high drawdown — bleed the line before starting.
A partially blocked foot valve or fouled check valve gives inconsistent results between runs.
Back-pressure differences between the calibration column and the normal suction source can shift the measured rate.
steps: Confirm the chemical, its concentration, and its specific gravity before starting — the calculated feed rate depends on all three.
Put on the PPE specified for the chemical (minimum: goggles, gloves, apron).
Verify the calibration column is clean, undamaged, and graduated in a readable unit (mL or L).
Isolate the pump suction from the day tank and open the valve so the pump draws from the calibration column.
Run the pump briefly to fill the suction line and expel air, then let the level settle.
Record the starting level in the column.
Start the pump and the stopwatch simultaneously. Run for a measured interval long enough for a readable drawdown — typically 1-5 minutes depending on pump size.
Stop the pump and stopwatch together and record the ending level.
Calculate the volume drawn down and convert to a rate: volume (L) ÷ time (min) × 1440 = L/day.
Repeat the run at least twice more. The three runs should agree closely; if they do not, investigate air, valve, or column issues before accepting a result.
Average the acceptable runs and compare to the target feed rate from the Chemical Feed Pump Rate calculator.
Adjust the stroke length and/or speed setting and repeat until the measured rate matches the target within your site's tolerance.
Restore the valve line-up: close the calibration column valve and reopen the day tank suction. CONFIRM the pump is drawing from the tank again before leaving.
Record in the Logbook: pump ID, chemical, date, measured rates for each run, final setting, and target rate. This record is the evidence that dosing is verified.
qualityControl: Require three consistent runs before accepting a calibration.
Track the setting-versus-rate relationship over time — a pump that needs progressively higher settings for the same output is wearing out.
Re-verify immediately after any maintenance on the pump, valves, or suction line.
troubleshooting: Drawdown varies widely between runs: air in the line, sticking check valve, or a leaking fitting.
Pump will not reach target rate at maximum setting: worn diaphragm/valves, excessive discharge pressure, or a blocked injection point.
Level in the column does not move: pump is air-locked or the suction valve line-up is wrong.
safetyNotes: Never leave the pump drawing from the calibration column — the column will run dry and air-lock the pump, interrupting treatment.
Assume the line is under pressure; relieve pressure before breaking any connection.
Have the chemical's safety data sheet and spill kit accessible before starting.
